newsitem.title: UK: Group accuses Europe of allowing illegal CFC trade.
newsitem.headline: Group accuses Europe of allowing illegal CFC trade.

text.p: Environmental campaigners on Wednesday accused Europe of haphazard enforcement of agreements aimed at protecting the ozone layer and said this was allowing widespread smuggling of ozone-depleting chemicals.

Continued trade in the chemicals -- chlorofluorocarbons or CFCs -- would seriously hit efforts to close the hole in the ozone layer, the London-based Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) said in a report.
"The illegal trade is significant," the report said. "Industry sources suggest that last year up to 20 percent of the total amount of CFCs in use were bought on the black market."

Citing dozens of environmental reports, the EIA said Europe had done little to control CFC smuggling. Countries that signed the 1987 Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer have agreed to phase out use of CFCs.
CFCs, widely used in refrigerants and elsewhere in industry, deplete the ozone layer through a chemical reaction. The ozone layer filters out harmful ultraviolet rays from the sun.
Holes have been found in both the northern and southern hemispheres and some scientists say they will lead to an increase in skin cancer rates. Radiation can also damage crops.
Because of the Montreal agreement, smuggling CFCs has become big business. Alternatives are often expensive or hard to make.

"Around 10,000 tonnes per year are estimated to be smuggled into the United States, and European smuggling is likely to be equal to at least 10 percent of the EU legal total of imports for 1994/95," the report said.

The EIA report, released to coincide with this week's meeting of the Parties to the Montreal Protocol in Costa Rica, said: "Enforcement within the EU is negligible and lacks any effective coordination."
European law was "haphazard, unclear and often poorly implemented at national level," it added.

"Almost all of the available evidence points to the Russian Federation as the biggest source." It quoted Environment Watch and the Washington-based Worldwatch Institute as saying 2,500 tonnes were illegally imported into the EU from Russia and Estonia in 1994.

"The EU must wake up to this problem fast. Far too often officials see the problem as one of tax revenue generation rather than environmental damage. It is essential that the EU matches the effective action that we've seen in the U.S."
